items.name: F against v graph to find force duration

items.name: Paper density from stack, whole-stack advantage
items.how: (i) Determine the density of paper in g cm^-3 from x = 210 mm, y = 42.7 mm, z = 297 mm and the stack mass (2); (ii) Explain why measuring the whole stack is better than one sheet (2).
items.ms: (i) rho = m / V with m = 2070 g, giving 0.777 g cm^-3 (3 s.f.). (ii) Thickness and mass measured are larger (1) so percentage uncertainty is smaller for the same uncertainty (1), or the single-sheet equivalent.

deps.name: Balance resolution and percentage uncertainty, paper stack

items.name: Circuit to measure electric motor power
items.how: Complete the circuit diagram (motor, battery and switch given) by adding components needed to determine the power of the motor.
items.ms: Battery/cell, switch, ammeter and voltmeter present (1); ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel with the motor (1); voltmeter across the battery accepted if no other resistive components.

items.name: Measuring height lifted accurately, with repeats
items.how: (i) Describe how to measure a single value of the height gained by the 1 kg mass in 10 s as accurately as possible, including any extra apparatus (4); the mark scheme also has (ii) a 2-mark justification for repeating readings, not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) Clamp the metre rule vertically (set square), place it close to the mass or attach a marker, read perpendicular to the scale (4). (ii) Random error (e.g. reaction time, parallax) causes variation (1); repeats allow a mean (1).

items.name: Motor efficiency from measured V, I, h, t
items.how: Explain how the student's measurements should be used to determine the efficiency of the motor as it lifts the mass.
items.ms: Power input = VI (1); useful power output = mgh / t (1); efficiency = (mgh / t) / (VI) (1, dependent on the first two). Energy version mgh / (VIt) also accepted.

deps.name: Circuit to measure electric motor power
Measuring height lifted accurately, with repeats

items.name: Laser safety precaution
items.how: Identify a health and safety issue caused by using a laser and how it may be dealt with.
items.ms: Laser light can damage or irritate the eye or dazzle (1); do not look into the beam, stand behind the laser, wear laser safety glasses or avoid reflective surfaces (1).

items.name: Minima separation and improving measurement
items.how: Hair diffraction pattern on a screen 2 m away: (i) describe how to determine an accurate distance between adjacent minima with a metre rule (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) an improvement to reduce uncertainty (2), not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) Measure between centres of several minima and divide by the number of gaps, or repeat for different adjacent pairs and take a mean (2). (ii) Increase hair-to-screen distance or use a longer wavelength to widen the pattern, or use a higher-resolution instrument such as vernier calipers, with reason (2).

items.name: Mean hair diameter and percentage uncertainty
items.how: Hair diameter d found with three lasers (76.0, 84.4, 77.1 micrometres): (i) determine the mean (2); (ii) determine the percentage uncertainty in the mean (2).
items.ms: (i) Mean = 79.2 micrometres, 3 s.f. (ii) Half range (accept furthest from mean) = 4.2 micrometres (1) giving 5.3% (6.5% if furthest value used) (1), ecf.

items.name: Hair versus copper breaking stress comparison
items.how: Deduce whether the suggestion that hair has the same breaking stress as copper (210 MPa) is correct, given hair 181 MPa with 6% uncertainty.
items.ms: Upper limit 181 x 1.06 = 192 MPa (1), below 210 MPa so the suggestion is not correct (1, dependent); OR percentage difference 14% exceeds 6%.

items.name: Sources of error in inverse square law
items.how: Explain how two sources of error can be reduced in a light intensity against distance investigation using a filament bulb, light meter and metre rule.
items.ms: Max 4 from two source/remedy pairs: cannot measure to the filament centre, so add the bulb radius to d; parallax in reading d, so use a set square or view perpendicular; background light, so use a dark room, cover the apparatus or subtract the background reading.

items.name: Inverse square law graph analysis, light intensity
items.how: Given I = k / d^2: (i) explain why I against 1/d^2 is a straight line through the origin (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) 1/d^2 values (2), (iii) graph plotting (5), (iv) gradient k (3) and (v) finding d from a given intensity (2), not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) I = k(1/d^2) is y = mx with constant gradient k and no intercept. (ii) 1/d^2 to 3 s.f. (iii) Labelled axes, sensible scales, plotting (2), line of best fit. (iv) Large-triangle gradient, k between 15.4 and 16.1 W (example 15.7), 2 or 3 s.f. with unit. (v) Use I = k / d^2, d between 1.96 and 2.01 m (ecf).

items.name: Instrument resolution and suitability, sphere diameter
items.how: Photograph of a measuring instrument used on a small metal sphere: (i) State its resolution (1); (ii) Explain why it is suitable for measuring the sphere diameter (2).
items.ms: (i) 0.1 mm (equivalents accepted). (ii) Percentage uncertainty is small (1) because the resolution is much less than the diameter, needing a comparison of resolution and measurement size (1).

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in sphere diameter
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a diameter reading of 20.5 +/- 0.05 mm.

items.name: Technique for accurate diameter readings
items.how: Describe how the student should use the measuring device so that repeated diameter measurements (and their mean) are as accurate as possible.
items.ms: Max 2 from: take readings in different orientations/positions; check for zero error; ensure the measurement is at the widest point.

items.name: Mean diameter and uncertainty, second sphere
items.how: Five diameter readings of a second sphere, one an anomaly (18.3 mm): (i) calculate the mean (2); (ii) calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mean (2).
items.ms: (i) Exclude the anomaly 18.3 mm, mean = 19.0 mm. (ii) Half range 0.1 mm (or furthest from mean) (1) giving 0.5% (0.53%) (1); ecf if all five values were used consistently.

items.name: Density of first metal sphere
items.how: Calculate the density of the first sphere (diameter 20.5 mm from part (b), mass 35.6 g from a top pan balance).
items.ms: V = 4/3 pi r^3 (1); rho = m / V (1); density = 7.89 x 10^3 kg m^-3 (1); given to 3 s.f. (1).

deps.name: Percentage uncertainty in sphere diameter

items.name: Same-metal test using density uncertainty
items.how: Determine whether two spheres could be made of the same metal, given the second sphere density 7.75 x 10^3 kg m^-3 with 2% uncertainty.
items.ms: Use the 2% to give a range (7.60 to 7.91 x 10^3 kg m^-3) (1); comparative statement consistent with the density from (e) (1).

deps.name: Density of first metal sphere

items.name: Procedure for force-extension data, spring
items.how: Describe what the student should do to obtain the data for a force-extension graph of a spring loaded with masses and measured with a metre rule.
items.ms: Force from mg or a newtonmeter (1); extension found by subtracting initial length from loaded length or using the bottom end of the spring (1); set square/pointer/eye level to control parallax and keep the rule vertical (1); range of masses giving multiple pairs of values (1).

items.name: Spring stiffness from force-extension gradient
items.how: Explain how the force-extension graph would be used to determine the stiffness of the spring.
items.ms: k = gradient = delta F / delta x (1); gradient calculated from the linear section of the graph (1).

deps.name: Procedure for force-extension data, spring

items.name: Measuring ring radius, electron diffraction
items.how: Describe how the student can accurately determine the radius of the first bright ring of an electron diffraction pattern on a curved screen.
items.ms: Use vernier calipers, dividers to transfer to a ruler, paper tape marks, or a flexible tape (1); measure the ring diameter and halve it (1); measure in several orientations and average (1); measure to the middle/brightest part of the ring or note the screen is curved (1).

items.name: Electron diffraction as evidence for wave nature
items.how: Explain how the diffraction pattern provides evidence for the wave nature of electrons.
items.ms: Diffracted electrons experience interference/superposition (must refer to electrons) (1); diffraction/interference is a wave property (1).

items.name: Electron diffraction results table, graph and d
items.how: Table of de Broglie wavelength and diffraction angle: (i) criticise the results (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) sin theta values and a lambda against sin theta graph (6), (iii) gradient (3) and (iv) explaining what the gradient represents (2), not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) Max 2 from: inconsistent s.f., only five sets, small range of values, no repeats. (ii) sin theta to 3 s.f., labelled axes (no unit for sin theta), scales, plotting (2), line of best fit. (iii) Large-triangle gradient 1.10 to 1.20 x 10^-10 m, 2 or 3 s.f., unit m. (iv) Compare n lambda = d sin theta with y = mx; gradient is d with n = 1.

items.name: Mass per unit length from standing wave
items.how: Calculate mu from sqrt(mg / mu) = f lambda using l = 1.25 m, f = 105 Hz, m = 0.25 kg and the standing wave pattern in the diagram.
items.ms: Use of sqrt(mg / mu) = f lambda (1); lambda from l = 1.5 lambda = 0.833 m (1); mu = 3.2 x 10^-4 kg m^-1 (1).

items.name: Uncertainty sources and reduction, vibrating string
items.how: (i) Identify two significant sources of uncertainty in the student's measurements (2); (ii) for each, describe an experimental technique the student could have used (4); text of (ii) is cut off in the input.
items.ms: Marked holistically. Sources: frequency (identifying nodes or maximum amplitude), length (parallax, string not straight, length to pulley), mass (zero error). Each needs a technique plus detail (max 4 from two pairs): repeat and average, approach resonance from above and below, set square or ruler in contact, zero the balance each time.

deps.name: Mass per unit length from standing wave

items.name: Resolutions table for acetate measurements
items.how: Complete a table of measuring instruments and resolutions needed to find the density of acetate sheets (mass, length and width, thickness); balance resolution given.
items.ms: Metre rule 0.1 cm and vernier calipers 0.1 mm (1 mark for both).

items.name: Method for accurate density of acetate
items.how: Describe a method to determine an accurate value for the density of acetate from a pack of 50 sheets with approximate dimensions given.
items.ms: Measure length and width in several positions and average (1); measure the thickness of at least 20 sheets (1); measure the mass of the same number of sheets (1); density = mass / (length x width x thickness) (1).

items.name: Thicker sheets reduce density uncertainty
items.how: Explain why using thicker sheets of acetate in the same method would reduce the uncertainty in the density.
items.ms: Absolute uncertainty (resolution) stays the same (1), so the percentage uncertainty in thickness/mass decreases (1, dependent).

deps.name: Method for accurate density of acetate

items.name: Reasons for variation in air column length
items.how: Suggest two reasons why the lengths l measured for the resonance of an air column in a tube varied.
items.ms: Two from: difficult to judge when the sound is loudest or hear the fork over background noise; tube moved or was not vertical when marking the water level.

items.name: Mean air column length and percentage uncertainty
items.how: Five readings of l (18.4, 18.0, 19.2, 19.4, 19.2 cm): (i) calculate the mean (2); (ii) calculate the percentage uncertainty in l (2).
items.ms: (i) Mean of all 5 values = 18.8 cm to 3 s.f. (ii) Half the range (or furthest from the mean) (1) giving about 4% (3.7% or 4.3%) (1).

items.name: Speed of sound from resonance length
items.how: Calculate the speed of sound from a 440 Hz tuning fork given that the standing wave has wavelength 4l.
items.ms: Use of v = f lambda with lambda = 4 x 0.188 m = 0.752 m (1); v = 331 m s^-1 (1); ecf from the mean l in (b).

deps.name: Mean air column length and percentage uncertainty

items.name: Consistency of measured speed with 343 m/s
items.how: Comment on whether the measured speed of sound is consistent with 343 m s^-1, given its percentage uncertainty equals that in l.
items.ms: Use the percentage uncertainty from (b)(ii) to find the relevant upper or lower limit of v from (c) (1) and compare with 343 m s^-1 (1); OR compare the percentage difference with the percentage uncertainty.

deps.name: Speed of sound from resonance length
Mean air column length and percentage uncertainty

items.name: Micrometer reading and percentage uncertainty, sphere
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the sphere diameter read from a micrometer shown in a diagram.
items.ms: Read diameter 17.90 mm (1); use half resolution 0.005 mm (1); percentage uncertainty 0.03% (1).

items.name: Micrometer precaution before use
items.how: State one precaution to take before using a micrometer.
items.ms: Check for zero error (do not overtighten also allowed).

items.name: Force readings explained; viscosity from Stokes law
items.how: Sphere pulled upwards through liquid at constant speed (force meter 0.20 N stationary, 0.29 N moving at 0.32 m s^-1): (i) explain why both readings are needed (3); the mark scheme also has (ii) calculating the viscosity (3), not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) Stationary reading = weight (minus upthrust); moving reading = weight + drag (minus upthrust); subtracting gives the drag (3). (ii) Drag = 0.09 N, use F = 6 pi eta r v with r = 0.00895 m, eta = 1.7 Pa s (3).

deps.name: Micrometer reading and percentage uncertainty, sphere

items.name: Most significant uncertainty in viscosity measurements
items.how: Assess which of the force, distance (25.0 cm) and time (0.78 s) measurements was the most significant source of uncertainty in viscosity, given the force meter resolution of 0.01 N.
items.ms: A comment assessing the uncertainty in each of force, distance and time (1 each), e.g. force 0.01 N gives about 11%, distance about 0.2%, time resolution 0.6% but reaction time could be about 25% of 0.78 s; conclusion justified with a numerical comparison (1).

deps.name: Force readings explained; viscosity from Stokes law

items.name: Straight-line graph of Va against 1/wavelength
items.how: Given eVa = hc / lambda + W, explain why a graph of Va against 1/lambda gives a straight line.
items.ms: Rearrange to Va = (hc/e)(1/lambda) + W/e and compare with y = mx + c (1); gradient = hc/e (1); h, c and e are all constants (1).

items.name: LED data: 1/lambda, graph, Planck constant
items.how: Table of LED wavelengths and activation p.d.: (i) complete 1/lambda values (2); (ii) plot Va against 1/lambda (5); (iii) determine the Planck constant (3); the mark scheme also has (iv) comparing with the accepted value (2), not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) 1/lambda correct and to 3 s.f. (1.52, 1.63, 1.69, 1.71, 1.89, 2.13 x 10^6 m^-1). (ii) Labelled axes, scales, two plotting marks, best-fit line. (iii) Large-triangle gradient (over half the line), gradient = hc/e, h between 6.65 and 6.85 x 10^-34 J s. (iv) Numerical comparison with 6.63 x 10^-34 J s and a consistent statement.

deps.name: Straight-line graph of Va against 1/wavelength

items.name: Effect of LED wavelength spread on accuracy
items.how: Discuss whether using the manufacturer's peak wavelength, not the wavelength emitted at the activation p.d., affects the accuracy of the Planck constant obtained.
items.ms: Manufacturer's wavelength is shorter than that emitted at Va (1) so 1/lambda is larger and the points shift right (1); then EITHER the shift is small/same for all points so gradient and h are unchanged (2) OR longer-wavelength points shift less so the gradient and h decrease (2).

deps.name: LED data: 1/lambda, graph, Planck constant

items.name: Average coin volume from diameter and thickness
items.how: Determine the average volume of one coin from a photograph of 20 coins laid against a ruler (diameter and stack thickness).
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: average diameter and thickness from all coins shown (2), volume of a cylinder from the averages (1), correct answer with unit (1).

items.name: Average coin density from mass of 20 coins
items.how: Determine the average density of the coins, given the mass of the 20 coins is 196 g.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: substitute mass and volume into density = mass / volume (1), answer in the accepted range with unit (1); ecf from (a); common slip is omitting the factor of 20.

deps.name: Average coin volume from diameter and thickness

items.name: Brass test using percentage uncertainty range
items.how: Determine whether the coins could be made from brass, density 8550 kg m^-3 +/- 2%.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: use the 2% to calculate at least one boundary of the density range (1) and make a statement comparing the value from (b) with that range (1); either conclusion can score if consistent with the value.

deps.name: Average coin density from mass of 20 coins

items.name: Displacement method for coin volume
items.how: Describe an alternative method for the average coin volume that avoids the systematic error from uneven surfaces, including how measuring equipment is used.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: displacement of water in a measuring cylinder, using several coins and dividing for an average volume (a single coin limited the marks to 2); correct use of a micrometer or vernier calipers also accepted.

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in measured angles
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in measured angles theta1 = 35 degrees and theta2 = 62 degrees read with a protractor.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: uncertainty of a single angle reading is half the resolution (0.5 degrees), then percentage uncertainty for each angle; an uncertainty of 1 degree accepted for a maximum of 2 marks.

items.name: Refractive index from sin graph gradient
items.how: Graph of sin theta2 against sin theta1: (i) explain why the gradient gives the refractive index (3); the report also describes (ii) using the gradient to determine the refractive index (not printed in the input; 5 marks derived from the 10-mark question total).
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: apply n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2 with theta1 in the block and n2 = 1 giving n sin theta1 = sin theta2, compare with y = mx so gradient = n (n = 1/gradient accepted if n1 = 1 is argued, with ecf in (ii)).

items.name: Non-zero intercept: cause and remedy
items.how: The line of best fit does not pass through the origin: describe a possible cause and how the student could reduce its effect.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: a valid cause specific to the protractor/block setup (normal not perpendicular to the flat surface or not straight, block moving, protractor zero misaligned) (1) and a remedy such as a set square, taping the block or marking its outline (1).

deps.name: Refractive index from sin graph gradient

items.name: Circuit to measure LDR resistance
items.how: Draw a circuit with an ammeter and voltmeter that could be used to determine the resistance of a light dependent resistor.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: supply with ammeter in series and voltmeter across the LDR, using the LDR symbol (with or without circle); 1 mark if the circuit would determine a resistance but the LDR symbol or component is wrong.

items.name: Accurate measurement of R and d
items.how: Describe a method the student could use to obtain accurate values of LDR resistance R and bulb-LDR distance d.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only); the report says there are three marking points about obtaining accurate measurements, not the overall method, but does not itemise them.

items.name: Sketch of intensity against distance
items.how: Sketch the relationship between light intensity I and distance d from a filament bulb on given axes.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: an inverse-square curve with decreasing gradient, asymptotic to both axes (2).

items.name: Intensity at 20 cm from 9.0 W bulb
items.how: Calculate the intensity on the LDR at d = 20 cm for a lamp of output power 9.0 W.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: area is the surface area of a sphere of radius d (4 pi d^2) (1), substitute into I = P / A (1), answer with unit (1); about 18 W m^-2 by calculation.

items.name: Control variable in LDR investigation
items.how: (i) Identify one control variable (1); (ii) state how it can be controlled (1); marked as a whole.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: a specific control variable, most suitably background light level, and a statement of how it is controlled; vague answers such as power, voltage or current, or the changing variable d, do not score.

items.name: Same release point gives same exit speed
items.how: Explain why releasing the sphere from the same position on the curved track ensures it always reaches the end with the same horizontal speed.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: use conservation of energy (loss of gravitational potential energy equals gain in kinetic energy) with the same release height and other quantities constant, so v is the same; the answer must be about speed, not just kinetic energy, and constant-acceleration equations cannot be used on the curve.

items.name: Criticise recorded H and D table
items.how: Criticise the recording of the table of H and D values for the rolling sphere.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: H not recorded to a consistent number of decimal places (matching ruler resolution); absence of repeats also credited at this stage.

items.name: D squared against H graph and sphere speed
items.how: (i) Calculate D^2 in the extra table column and plot D^2 (y) against H (x) (6); (ii) use the graph, with gradient = 2v^2 / g, to determine v (3); visible brackets total 9 of the question's 16 marks, so some marks are not visible in the input.
items.ms: No mark scheme in the input (examiners' report only). Report: D^2 to 2 s.f. with squared unit, axis labels with units using /, sensible scales, plots within 1 mm, balanced best-fit line through the origin; gradient from over half the line, then v from gradient = 2v^2 / g using the graph rather than table values.

deps.name: Criticise recorded H and D table

items.name: Micrometer reading, uncertainty and error reduction
items.how: Micrometer reading of ruler thickness t shown in a diagram: (i) State t (1); (ii) Determine the percentage uncertainty (2); (iii) Explain how to reduce a source of error (2).
items.ms: (i) 1.72 mm. (ii) Half resolution / measurement x 100%: 0.005 / 1.72 = 0.29% (full resolution scores 1 mark only). (iii) Check zero error to remove systematic error, OR use the ratchet to avoid over-tightening/deformation (2).

items.name: Mass of ruler by principle of moments
items.how: Describe how to determine an accurate mass of a ruler balanced on a pivot, using a 20 g mass and the apparatus shown.
items.ms: Add the 20 g mass at a distance and find the new balance point (1); measure distances from the pivot to the ruler's centre of gravity and to the 20 g mass (1); use the principle of moments to find the mass (1); repeat with different positions of the 20 g mass and average (1).

items.name: Convex lens purpose; keeping intensity constant
items.how: Solar cell illuminated by a bulb and lens: (i) Explain the purpose of the convex lens (2); (ii) Describe two more ways to keep the light intensity on the cell constant (2).
items.ms: (i) Lens gives a parallel beam or concentrates light on the cell (1) because light from the bulb spreads out / to increase or even out the intensity (1). (ii) Max two from: control background light, keep the cell at the same distance, keep it at the same angle to the bulb.

items.name: Solar cell I-V circuit and fixed resistor
items.how: (i) Add an ammeter and a voltmeter to the circuit diagram for measuring p.d. against current for a solar cell (2); (ii) Suggest a reason for using a fixed resistor (1).
items.ms: (i) Ammeter in series with the cell, resistor and variable resistor (1); voltmeter in parallel with the solar cell (1). (ii) Limits the maximum current / avoids short-circuiting the cell.

items.name: Advantages of solar cell powered garden pump
items.how: Describe two advantages of using solar cells to power a small garden water pump; classed OFF because energy resources and renewable power are not in the 2018 spec taxonomy.
items.ms: Max two from: no greenhouse gas emissions or less need for fossil fuels; renewable energy source; sunlight is free; no mains wiring needed / usable where there is no mains electricity.
path: Older-spec content not on the 2018 spec

items.name: Vernier calipers versus ruler; reducing error
items.how: Measuring ring diameters on an electron diffraction screen: (i) give two reasons vernier calipers are more appropriate than a transparent ruler (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) a technique to reduce error in the measurement (2), not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) Max two from: smaller resolution/uncertainty, no parallax error, tips easier to align with the rings on a curved surface. (ii) Repeat and calculate a mean (1); measure the diameter in different orientations (1); checking zero error scores 1 if nothing else awarded.

items.name: Mean of a, its uncertainty, benefit of graph
items.how: Table of V, lambda and a = V lambda^2 for three accelerating voltages: (i) determine the mean a (2); (ii) the percentage uncertainty in the mean (2); the mark scheme also has (iii) why a line of best fit graph is better than a mean (2), not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) Mean of all three = 1.22 x 10^-18 m^2 V (3 s.f.). (ii) Half range (or furthest from mean) (1) giving about 9% (8.6%) (1), ecf. (iii) Max two from: more pairs of values used, line of best fit averages and identifies anomalies, gradient ignores systematic error / intercept reveals it.

items.name: Planck constant from electron diffraction constant
items.how: (i) Calculate h in J s from a = h^2 / (2 e m_e) when a = 1.46 x 10^-18 m^2 V (2); (ii) Comment on the accuracy of h given its 6% uncertainty (2).
items.ms: (i) h = sqrt(2 e m_e a) = 6.52 x 10^-34 J s. (ii) Upper limit 6.92 x 10^-34 J s is above 6.63 x 10^-34 J s (or percentage difference 1.7% is less than 6%), so the value is accurate (2, ecf).

items.name: Health and safety with hanging mass and cord
items.how: Identify a health and safety issue and how it may be dealt with, for a 1.2 kg mass hung from an elastic cord between two stands.
items.ms: A hazard (cord may snap, stands may topple, mass may fall) (1) with a matching remedy (goggles or screen, clamp stands or weight the bases, keep feet away or cushion under the mass) (1, dependent).

items.name: Sources of uncertainty in angle and length
items.how: Angle theta measured with a protractor and length x with a metre rule: (i) identify two sources of uncertainty (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) one modification to reduce a stated source (1), not printed in the input.
items.ms: Marked holistically. Sources: parallax with rule or protractor, error from cord thickness, misaligned zero or moving rule/protractor, extra force on cord/mass. Reduction (linked to a stated source): view perpendicular or hold close, mark the cord centre, clamp the rule or protractor, avoid touching the cord/mass.

items.name: Cos(theta/2) against 1/extension graph to find g
items.how: Given cos(theta/2) = (m g / k)(1 / delta x): (i) explain why a graph of cos(theta/2) against 1/delta x gives g (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) calculating 1/delta x and plotting the graph (6), (iii) gradient (3) and (iv) g from the gradient (2), not printed in the input.
items.ms: (i) Compare with y = mx: gradient = m g / k, so g = gradient x k / m. (ii) 1/delta x to 3 s.f., labelled axes, sensible scales (2), plotting, line of best fit. (iii) Large-triangle gradient between 0.076 and 0.079 m, 2 or 3 s.f. (iv) g = gradient x k / m, about 9.43 m s^-2 (example), with correct unit, ecf.

deps.name: Sources of uncertainty in angle and length

items.name: Safety issues, breaking rubber band
items.how: Identify two health and safety issues and how to deal with each (4 marks) for a rubber band pulled by a force meter on a stand; part (ii), not in the extracted text, appears in the MS as a 2-mark method for applying and calculating the breaking force.
items.ms: (i) Two hazards with controls, 1 mark each: stand toppling (clamp the base or add a heavy mass) and band snapping into eye or face (wear eye protection). (ii) Add masses gradually until the band breaks, then F = mg.

items.name: Reason for repeating freezer breaking-force tests
items.how: Explain why it is appropriate to repeat the breaking-force measurement on five identical rubber bands cooled to -10 C (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: Repeating reduces the effect of random error (systematic error not accepted), caused by variation in the temperature of the rubber bands; 1 mark each.

items.name: Control variable, ball bouncing from slope
items.how: (i) State one control variable (1) and (ii) explain why it must be controlled (2), for a ball dropped onto a slope with landing distance x measured against slope angle theta.
items.ms: (i) Drop height of the ball, or initial velocity (accept released from rest). (ii) Linked to the stated variable: height affects GPE or time accelerating (or initial velocity affects KE), so the impact velocity or KE would vary.

items.name: Criticise recorded slope angle and distance data
items.how: Criticise the recording of a short table of slope angle theta and landing distance x (Criticise, 3 marks).
items.ms: Any three: values not recorded to consistent decimal places, no evidence of repeats, too few data sets for a reliable graph, the x reading of 20.5 does not follow the trend.

items.name: Reduce landing-point error with extra apparatus
items.how: Explain one modification, including additional apparatus, to reduce the error from being unable to judge where a fast-moving ball lands (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: Either a camera recording the motion that can be viewed in slow motion, or a tray of sand for the ball to land in so it stays still or leaves an indentation; 1 mark for the apparatus, 1 for why it helps.

items.name: Measuring air column length s accurately
items.how: Describe a method to determine one value of s (air column in a transparent tube below an ultrasonic transducer) as accurately as possible using a metre rule; additional apparatus allowed (Describe, 3 marks).
items.ms: Clamp the rule vertically close to the tube (check with a set square or spirit level); line the zero up with the transducer base or water surface, or measure to both and subtract; view the rule perpendicularly or use a set square. Any valid method accepted.

items.name: Show speed of ultrasound from echo trace
items.how: Show that v is about 330 m/s using an oscilloscope trace of emitted and reflected pulses (0.5 ms per division) and s = 49.7 cm (Show that, 4 marks).
items.ms: t = 6 divisions x 0.5 ms = 3 ms; use v = distance/time with the path 2s (or t/2); v = 2 x 0.497 m / 3x10^-3 s = 331 m/s. Bald answer scores 0 and use of v = f x wavelength is not accepted.

items.name: Mean and percentage uncertainty of sound speed
items.how: (i) Determine the mean of four values of v (2) and (ii) the percentage uncertainty in that mean (2) (Determine).
items.ms: (i) Mean = 341 m/s to 3 s.f. (ii) Half range = 6 m/s (or furthest value from the mean), then 6/341 x 100 = 1.8%, with ecf from (i).

items.name: Consistency of measured and accepted water sound speed
items.how: Deduce, with a calculation, whether 1444 m/s (4% uncertainty) is consistent with the accepted 1481 m/s for the speed of sound in water (Deduce, 2 marks).
items.ms: Either upper limit 1444 x 1.04 = about 1502 m/s is above 1481 so consistent, or percentage difference 2.5% is less than the 4% uncertainty so consistent; 1 mark for calculation, 1 for conclusion.

items.name: Micrometer uncertainty and accurate diameter technique
items.how: (i) Determine the percentage uncertainty in a single micrometer reading of 0.27 mm (2); (ii) explain another technique, besides averaging, for an accurate wire diameter (2).
items.ms: (i) Half resolution 0.005 mm / 0.27 mm x 100 = 1.9 or 2%. (ii) Either check and correct for zero error (removes systematic error) or use the ratchet (reduces random error); second mark dependent on the first.

items.name: Purpose of fixed resistor in resistance circuit
items.how: Explain why a fixed resistor is included in the ammeter-voltmeter circuit used to find the resistance between X and Y on a wire loop (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: It limits the maximum current, so the wire or circuit does not overheat (or there is no short circuit, or the ammeter or battery is not damaged).

items.name: Resistivity from R/L against L graph
items.how: (i) Explain how a graph of R/L against L gives rho, given R/L = -kL + rho/A (2); the extracted text stops at (i), but the MS shows further parts: complete a table of R/L (2), plot the graph (5), find k from the gradient (3) and find rho from the y-intercept (3).
items.ms: (i) Compare with y = mx + c, so rho/A is the y-intercept and rho = intercept x A. Rest per MS: R/L to 3 s.f. (19.4 down to 11.7 ohm/m), labelled axes, scales, plotting and best-fit line, k about 15.3 ohm m^-2 from a large-triangle gradient, then intercept (about 20.9 ohm/m) x A with A = pi d^2/4 (d = 0.27 mm) gives rho about 1.2x10^-6 ohm m.

deps.name: Micrometer uncertainty and accurate diameter technique
Purpose of fixed resistor in resistance circuit

items.name: Source of uncertainty in echo time
items.how: State one source of uncertainty in students' hand-timed values of the echo delay t (State, 1 mark).
items.ms: Reaction time, or the timer not reset to zero.

items.name: Handling echo times and anomalous reading
items.how: (i) Explain why both the students' suggestion (use all five t values) and the teacher's (discard student 4's 0.75 s) are reasonable (Explain, 4); the MS also shows (ii)-(iv) in the same question: mean time, percentage uncertainty and maximum distance using v = 330 m/s (8 more marks).
items.ms: (i) Students: range of 0.16 s is comparable to reaction time. Teacher: other four values span only 0.04 s (uncertainty 0.02 s) so 0.75 s is far outside. (ii) Mean 0.89 s from four values (0.86 s from five). (iii) Half range 0.02 s gives 2%. (iv) s = 330 x 0.91/2 = about 150 m maximum distance.

items.name: Method to find angle for maximum range
items.how: Describe an experimental method to find the launch angle at which the range d of a launched sphere is greatest, given d = (v^2/g) sin 2 theta (Describe, 4 marks).
items.ms: Measure d with a ruler and theta with a protractor; repeat at each angle and take mean d; plot d against theta (or keep changing theta until d falls) to locate the maximum; take readings at smaller angle steps around the maximum.

items.name: Why maximum range occurs below 45 degrees
items.how: Suggest two reasons why the measured maximum range occurred at an angle below the predicted 45 degrees (Suggest, 2 marks).
items.ms: Any two: parallax when reading angle or distance, angle not zero when the launcher is horizontal, air resistance reducing the speed, launch speed not constant because of angle-dependent friction in the launcher tube.

items.name: Check rod uniform diameter by balancing
items.how: Explain how suspending the 30 cm aluminium rod from a thread could confirm it has uniform diameter (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: The rod balances horizontally with the thread at 15 cm (the middle); because mass or moments either side are equal, so the centre of mass is at 15 cm.

items.name: Rod potential divider and cell terminal p.d.
items.how: (i) Read the p.d. V at x = 30 cm from the plotted graph (1); (ii) given the measured rod resistance (extract garbled), determine the terminal p.d. of the cell (Determine, 2).
items.ms: (i) V between 0.40 and 0.45 V from the line. (ii) Ratio of resistance equals ratio of p.d. (or V = IR with rod 0.070 ohm): terminal p.d. = V x R_total/R_rod = 0.41 x 0.27/0.070 = 1.6 V; ecf from (i).

items.name: Why more readings improve terminal p.d. value
items.how: Explain why taking more than three readings of V and x could improve the accuracy of the terminal p.d. value (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: More readings make the line of best fit more accurate, giving a more accurate p.d. across the rod at 30 cm and hence a better terminal p.d.

deps.name: Rod potential divider and cell terminal p.d.

items.name: Test whether rotation constant k is constant
items.how: Determine whether a table of angle of rotation against sucrose concentration (fixed 10 cm depth) supports k being constant, given angle = k x concentration x depth (Determine, 3 marks).
items.ms: Calculate angle/concentration (or k) for two pairs of values, then for at least one more pair, and make a comparative statement consistent with the values.

items.name: Why polarimeter light source needs low power
items.how: Explain why the polarimeter light source should have a low power (Explain, 3 marks).
items.ms: A higher power lamp heats the solution; heating causes expansion or evaporation; this changes the concentration or density of the sucrose solution.

items.name: Graphical method to determine k
items.how: Describe a graphical method the student could have used to determine k (Describe, 3 marks).
items.ms: Compare angle = k x concentration x depth with y = mx; plot angle against concentration (or against concentration x depth); k from the gradient (divided by depth in the first case).

items.name: Advantage of visible-light photoelectric apparatus
items.how: Explain an advantage of using photoelectric apparatus whose metal works with visible light, when other metals need higher photon energies (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: Higher photon energy means higher frequency light such as ultraviolet; ultraviolet carries increased risk, whereas visible light is no or low risk.

items.name: Work done on electron by 1.58 V
items.how: Calculate the work done on an emitted electron by a p.d. of 1.58 V (Calculate, 2 marks).

items.name: Plot stopping p.d. against 1/wavelength, find h
items.how: (i) Calculate 1/lambda in the spare column and plot stopping p.d. V against 1/lambda (6); (ii) determine the Planck constant from the gradient using h = gradient x e / c (Determine, 3).
items.ms: (i) 1/lambda to 2-3 s.f. (2.63 down to 1.61 x10^6 m^-1), axes with quantities and units, sensible scales, plotting (2), best-fit line. (ii) Large-triangle gradient (about 1.2x10^-6 V m), then h = gradient x e / c; accepted h between 6.2 and 7.0 x10^-34 J s.

items.name: Improving accuracy of Planck constant experiment
items.how: Suggest two modifications that would improve the accuracy of the Planck constant found from the filter and stopping-potential experiment (Suggest, 2 marks).
items.ms: Any two: block external light, use a larger range of wavelengths, use filters with a narrower frequency band, use LEDs of known frequency, use a more sensitive ammeter.

items.name: Apparatus for temperature variation and timing
items.how: (i) State apparatus to vary the oil temperature (1) and (ii) apparatus to time the flow through a funnel (1) (State).
items.ms: (i) Heating or cooling apparatus, e.g. hot plate or ice/water bath. (ii) Timing apparatus, e.g. stopwatch or stop clock.

items.name: Justify digital over liquid-in-glass thermometer
items.how: Justify the student's choice of a digital thermometer over a liquid-in-glass thermometer (Justify, 2 marks).
items.ms: Digital thermometer has higher resolution (e.g. 0.1 C) or no parallax error; so it has a lower (percentage) uncertainty. Calculating percentage uncertainties for both earns MP1.

items.name: Control variable and its control, oil flow
items.how: (i) Identify one control variable (1) and (ii) describe how it can be controlled (1) in the oil funnel investigation.
items.ms: (i) e.g. volume or mass of oil (not temperature of oil or room). (ii) A matching method, e.g. check the volume in the measuring cylinder each time or measure the mass on a balance.

items.name: Rate of flow and improving timing accuracy
items.how: (i) State how the rate of flow should be calculated (1); (ii) describe how the same apparatus could give a more accurate rate of flow than timing from start of pouring to the last drop (Describe, 2).
items.ms: (i) Rate of flow = volume/time. (ii) Any two: start timing after pouring (marked start volume), stop before the funnel empties (fixed volume or marker), record volume after a fixed time, repeat and average, or use light gates and an electronic timer to avoid reaction time.

items.name: Best-fit line for LED intensity graph
items.how: Add a line of best fit to the plotted graph of LED light intensity against p.d. (Add, 1 mark).
items.ms: A curved line of best fit.

items.name: LED threshold p.d. and minimum electron energy
items.how: (i) Give the p.d. at which the LED starts to conduct (1) and (ii) calculate the minimum energy transferred to an electron for light to be emitted (Calculate, 2).
items.ms: (i) Read the minimum p.d. from own line on the graph. (ii) W = VQ with Q = 1.6x10^-19 C, e.g. 1.8 V gives 2.9x10^-19 J; accepted range 2.5 to 3.0 x10^-19 J.

deps.name: Best-fit line for LED intensity graph

items.name: Planck constant from LED wavelength and energy
items.how: Calculate the Planck constant for a second LED of wavelength 625 nm with minimum electron energy 3.1x10^-19 J (Calculate, 3 marks).
items.ms: c = f x lambda gives f = 4.8x10^14 Hz; E = hf gives h = 6.5x10^-34 J s. Using E = hc/lambda directly earns MP1 and MP2.

items.name: Effect of non-monochromatic LED on h
items.how: Explain how the LED not producing monochromatic light would affect the calculated Planck constant (Explain, 3 marks).
items.ms: There is a range of wavelengths or frequencies so an uncertainty in lambda; a longer wavelength would give a larger h (converse for shorter); so there is an uncertainty or range of possible values of h.

deps.name: Planck constant from LED wavelength and energy

items.name: Reduce uncertainty in minimum LED p.d.
items.how: Explain how the student could reduce the uncertainty in her value of the minimum p.d. (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: Take extra readings at smaller p.d. increments, particularly between 1.5 and 2.0 V (or use a data logger); this gives a more accurate best-fit line and so a more accurate x-intercept.

deps.name: LED threshold p.d. and minimum electron energy

items.name: Circuit to measure solar cell power output
items.how: Complete a circuit diagram that would allow the power output of the solar cell to be determined (Complete, 2 marks).
items.ms: Voltmeter in parallel with the solar cell only (parallel to the resistor only is accepted if there are no other resistive components); ammeter in series with the solar cell and resistor. Extra cells lose the second mark.

items.name: Keeping light intensity constant on solar cell
items.how: Describe how the student could keep the light intensity incident on the solar cell constant (Describe, 2 marks).
items.ms: Max two: keep the lamp-to-cell distance the same, keep the angle of the cell to the light the same, block or control background light or avoid shadows on the cell.

items.name: Method to raise solar cell temperature
items.how: State a method to increase the temperature of the solar cell (State, 1 mark).
items.ms: A suitable method, not just a named heat source, e.g. immerse in a water bath or clamp a fixed distance from a hair dryer.

items.name: Solar cell power output from V and I
items.how: Calculate the power output of the solar cell from 2.74 V and 45 mA (Calculate, 2 marks).

items.name: Solar cell efficiency at room temperature
items.how: Calculate the efficiency of the 60 mm x 60 mm solar cell given incident intensity 200 W m^-2 (Calculate, 3 marks).
items.ms: Input power = intensity x area = 200 x (0.060)^2 = 0.72 W; efficiency = useful power output / total power input = 0.12/0.72 = 0.17 (17%); ecf from (d).

deps.name: Solar cell power output from V and I

items.name: Criticise temperature data and power analysis
items.how: (i) Criticise a table of temperature, V and I readings (Criticise, 2); the MS also shows a part (ii) worth 3 marks (question text not in the extract) on finding the power change per degree.
items.ms: (i) Any two: too few readings, too small a temperature range, inconsistent temperature intervals, inconsistent d.p. in current. (ii) Calculate power at each temperature, plot power against temperature and use the gradient (or plot temperature against power and take 1/gradient).

items.name: Method to determine maximum friction force
items.how: Describe how the student can determine the maximum frictional force F for a rubber block pulled over concrete by slotted masses via a pulley (Describe, 2 marks).
items.ms: Increase the slotted masses until the block just starts to slide; then find F as the weight of the slotted masses using mg (or measure the weight with a newton meter).

items.name: Normal force values and F against N graph
items.how: (i) Explain how the normal force values N are calculated from the added mass m and the 250 g block (2); (ii) plot a graph of F on the y-axis against N on the x-axis (5).
items.ms: (i) Add 250 g (0.25 kg, or 2.45 N) to m, then use W = mg. (ii) Axes labelled with quantities and units, sensible scales, plotting (2), line of best fit.

items.name: Coefficient of friction from graph gradient
items.how: Determine a value for the constant mu in F = mu N (Determine, 3 marks).
items.ms: Gradient from a large triangle (e.g. 0.556); mu in range 0.54 to 0.59; given to 2 or 3 s.f. with no unit.

deps.name: Normal force values and F against N graph

items.name: Why tyre makers test rubber friction
items.how: Suggest why a tyre manufacturer needs to carry out similar friction tests on samples of tyre rubber (Suggest, 2 marks).
items.ms: To check the tyres give enough friction or grip (including on wet, icy or loose surfaces); so a car can stop in a safe distance or time and not skid.

items.name: Varying thermistor temperature from 10 to 100 C
items.how: Describe how the student varied the thermistor temperature between 100 C and 10 C (Describe, 2 marks).
items.ms: A suitable heating method (e.g. water bath, kettle) and a suitable cooling method (e.g. ice bath, freezer), 1 mark each.

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in voltmeter reading
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the voltmeter reading shown in a photograph (Calculate, 2 marks).
items.ms: Uncertainty = half resolution = 0.005 V; percentage uncertainty = 0.005/6.85 x 100 = 0.07%. Using full resolution (0.01 V, 0.15%) earns MP2 only.

items.name: Thermistor voltage at 0 C and resistance
items.how: (i) Estimate V at 0 C by extending the V against theta graph (2); (ii) calculate the thermistor resistance at 0 C using the 12 V supply and 4.7 kohm fixed resistor (3).
items.ms: (i) Best-fit line extended to the V axis, value between 8.2 and 8.6 V. (ii) 12 V = sum of p.d.s, V = IR (I = 3.6 V / 4.7 kohm = 7.7x10^-4 A, R = 8.4 V / I) giving about 1.1x10^4 ohm with unit; potential divider ratio also accepted; ecf from (i).

items.name: Test V inversely proportional to kelvin temperature
items.how: Determine whether the student is correct that V is inversely proportional to temperature in kelvin (Determine, 2 marks).
items.ms: Calculate V x T (T in kelvin) for at least two pairs of values from the graph or table (e.g. 1170 and 1730 V K) and give a conclusion consistent with them; no mark if temperatures are not converted to kelvin.

deps.name: Thermistor voltage at 0 C and resistance

items.name: Why microwave intensity varies with plate position
items.how: Explain why the microwave intensity at the receiver varies as the glass plate distance d is varied (Explain, 3 marks).
items.ms: Path (or phase) difference between waves reflected from the metal and glass plates; the reflected waves superpose at the receiver; changing d changes the path difference, giving constructive then destructive interference.

items.name: Microwave wavelength and frequency from maxima
items.how: (i) Determine the wavelength from five successive maxima positions d (3); the MS also shows (ii), 2 marks, for calculating the frequency (question text not in the extract).
items.ms: (i) Mean spacing of maxima 1.38 cm; wavelength = 2 x spacing = 2.8 cm to 2 s.f. (ii) c = f x lambda gives f = 1.1x10^10 Hz, ecf from (i).

items.name: Method for maximum breaking force of nylon
items.how: Describe a method to determine the maximum force a nylon fishing line can withstand before breaking (Describe, 4 marks).
items.ms: Secure one end of the nylon; hang slotted masses from the other end; increase the force or mass until it breaks; use F = mg (or a force meter to weigh the masses). A diagram can earn the first two marks.

items.name: Safety issue and control, nylon breaking test
items.how: Identify one safety issue with the nylon breaking investigation and how to deal with it (Identify, 2 marks).
items.ms: An appropriate hazard and a matching control, e.g. masses falling on feet (keep feet clear) or snapped nylon hitting eyes (wear safety glasses).

items.name: Diameter uncertainty and stress before and after water
items.how: (i) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mean diameter from five readings (3); the MS also shows (ii), 5 marks (question text not in the extract), comparing ultimate tensile stress before and after the nylon absorbs water.
items.ms: (i) Mean 0.55 mm, half range 0.02 mm, percentage uncertainty 3.6%. (ii) A = pi r^2 and stress = F/A before (65.8 N, 4.1x10^8 Pa) and after (57.8 N, 3.5x10^8 Pa), percentage change about 15%, with a comparative statement.

items.name: Criticise rebound heights and plot r against h
items.how: (i) Criticise a table of release height h and rebound height r (Criticise, 2); (ii) plot a graph of r on the y-axis against h on the x-axis (5).
items.ms: (i) Any two: inconsistent decimal places in r, no repeat readings, all values should be to the nearest mm (3 d.p.). (ii) Axes with quantities and units, sensible scales, plotting (2), line of best fit.

items.name: Derive impact speed and gradient equals e squared
items.how: (i) Show that u = sqrt(2gh) (Show that, 2); (ii) with e = v/u, show the graph gradient equals e^2 (3; question text truncated in the extract, content from MS).
items.ms: (i) mgh = 1/2 m u^2 then rearrange (use of suvat not accepted). (ii) v = sqrt(2gr), so e = sqrt(r/h) and gradient = delta r / delta h = e^2.

deps.name: Criticise rebound heights and plot r against h

items.name: Identify cube metal from coefficient of restitution
items.how: Determine whether the cube could be stainless steel (0.63 < e < 0.93) or cast iron (0.3 < e < 0.6) (Determine, 3 marks).
items.ms: Large-triangle gradient (or r/h) gives e^2 between 0.51 and 0.56, so e about 0.73 (0.71 to 0.75); choose stainless steel as it lies in that range.

deps.name: Criticise rebound heights and plot r against h
Derive impact speed and gradient equals e squared

items.name: Effect of ramp friction on coefficient of restitution
items.how: Explain how friction between the cube and the ramp would affect the value obtained for e (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: Friction reduces the speed or dissipates energy (smaller acceleration), so r is lower for a given h; so the gradient and the obtained value of e would be smaller (second mark dependent on first).

deps.name: Derive impact speed and gradient equals e squared

items.name: Card length measurement and percentage uncertainty
items.how: (i) Determine an accurate length of the glider card from an actual-size drawing (2) and (ii) calculate the percentage uncertainty in that value (2) (Determine, Calculate).
items.ms: (i) Measure top and bottom edges and take the mean: 6.5 cm (0.065 m). (ii) Half range 0.1 cm gives 1.5% (or half ruler resolution gives 0.77% for a single value); approach must match (i); ecf allowed.

items.name: Glider velocity, momentum and conservation check
items.how: (i) Calculate the missing velocity and momentum values for the joined gliders from a 10.5 cm card, 205 ms and 0.274 kg (Calculate, 4); the MS also shows (ii), 2 marks, concluding on conservation of momentum (question text not in the extract).
items.ms: (i) v = s/t = 0.105 m / 0.205 s = 0.512 m/s and p = mv = 0.140 kg m/s, both to 3 s.f. (ii) Percentage difference between momentum before and after about 2.1%, small, so momentum is conserved.

items.name: Variable hand force effect on momentum uncertainty
items.how: Discuss how starting glider A with a hand force, with mean light-gate times from repeats, affected the uncertainty in the calculated momentum (Discuss, 3 marks).
items.ms: The force (or its duration) could differ each time; so the time, velocity, acceleration or momentum of glider A differs between repeats; increasing the uncertainty in momentum (third mark dependent on either of the first two).

deps.name: Glider velocity, momentum and conservation check

items.name: Light gates and data logger versus stopwatch
items.how: Explain the advantage of light gates and a data logger over a stopwatch for timing the gliders (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: They remove human reaction time (a stopwatch includes it); this reduces the effect of random error or the uncertainty in the time.

items.name: Justify resistivity falling as salt mass increases
items.how: Justify the prediction that the resistivity of a salt solution decreases as the mass of dissolved salt m increases, given that salt ions are charge carriers (Justify, 3 marks).
items.ms: More salt gives more charge carriers (n); using I = nAvq, current increases; resistance (and so resistivity) decreases (third mark dependent on either earlier mark).

items.name: Graph of 1/resistivity against salt mass
items.how: (i) Explain how the graph of 1/rho against m supports the conclusion that resistivity is inversely proportional to mass of salt (Explain, 3); the MS also shows (ii), 2 marks, criticising the data (question text not in the extract).
items.ms: (i) Points lie on a straight line, the line passes through the origin, so 1/rho is proportional to m (third mark dependent). (ii) Only four data points and a small range of masses (nothing below 5 g or above 8 g).

items.name: Measuring object and image distances for lens
items.how: (i) Describe a method to measure the object distance u and image distance v using a metre rule (3); the MS also shows (ii), 2 marks, on a source of uncertainty and how to reduce it (question text not in the extract).
items.ms: (i) Measure vertically from paper to liquid surface (v), from paper to the filament, subtract to find u (or measure lens to filament directly with the zero at the lens). (ii) A source such as parallax, rule not vertical, zero error or filament inside the bulb, with a fix such as a set square, checking the zero or measuring to the bulb middle.

items.name: Lens power and refractive index of liquid
items.how: (i) Calculate the missing lens power P from P = 1/u + 1/v (Calculate, 2); the MS also shows (ii), 3 marks, using the mean power and lens radius to find the refractive index (question text not in the extract).
items.ms: (i) P = 1/0.615 + 1/0.374 = 4.30 D to 3 s.f. (ii) P = (n_lens - n_air)/(n_air x r) with n_air = 1, so n_lens = P r + 1 = 1.3 using mean P = 4.297 D and r = 0.070 m.

deps.name: Measuring object and image distances for lens

items.name: Criticise recorded beam deflection results
items.how: Criticise the recording of the table of force F and deflection d for the plastic beam (Criticise, 2 marks).
items.ms: No repeat measurements; inconsistent decimal places for d (not all recorded to the same resolution).

items.name: Plot beam deflection d against force F
items.how: Plot a graph of d on the y-axis against F on the x-axis on the grid provided (Plot, 5 marks).
items.ms: Axes labelled with quantities and units, sensible scales, plotting (2 marks), line of best fit.

items.name: Graph gradient and bending modulus of beam
items.how: (i) Show that the gradient equals l^3/(4wh^3E) from E = l^3 F/(4wh^3 d) (Show that, 2); the MS also shows (ii) determine the gradient (2) and (iii) determine E (2), question text truncated in the extract.
items.ms: (i) Rearrange to d = (l^3/4wh^3E) F and compare with y = mx (or d/F = l^3/(4wh^3E)). (ii) Large-triangle gradient in range 1.30 to 1.40 x10^-4 m/N. (iii) E from the gradient with l = 0.30 m, w = 0.020 m, h = 0.010 m gives 2.41 to 2.60 GPa (about 2.5 GPa).

deps.name: Plot beam deflection d against force F

items.name: Why thinner beam improves deflection measurement
items.how: Justify the teacher's statement that a beam with a smaller h would improve the measurement of d (Justify, 2 marks).
items.ms: A thinner beam gives a larger d for the same force; this reduces the percentage uncertainty in d (second mark dependent on first).

items.name: Safety issue using glass instead of plastic
items.how: Explain a safety issue caused by repeating the investigation with a glass rod instead of a plastic beam (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: Identify the relevant physics and a safety issue, e.g. glass is brittle and snaps with sharp edges causing cuts, or glass is stiffer so a larger mass is needed which could injure feet if dropped.

items.name: Instrument for measuring cube dimensions
items.how: Identify a suitable measuring instrument for the length, width and height of a small metal cube (Identify, 1 mark).
items.ms: Any one of: vernier calipers, digital calipers, micrometer screw gauge.

items.name: Why mean width has larger uncertainty
items.how: Suggest why the uncertainty in the mean width is larger than for the mean length and height, using a table of three repeats (Suggest, 1 mark).
items.ms: Any one: the 20.0 mm reading is an outlier or anomaly (or misread), the cube is not uniform, the cube has been damaged.

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in mean cube length
items.how: Determine the percentage uncertainty in the mean length from three repeat measurements (Determine, 2 marks).
items.ms: Uncertainty = half the range (or maximum difference from the mean) = 0.1 mm; percentage uncertainty = 0.1/20.2 x 100 = 0.5%, to 1 or 2 s.f.

items.name: Cube density and identifying the metal
items.how: (i) Show that the density is about 8800 kg m^-3 from mass 72.8 g and the mean dimensions (Show that, 4); the MS also shows (ii), 3 marks, identifying the metal from a density table using a 2% uncertainty (question text not in the extract).
items.ms: (i) Convert mm to m and g to kg, V = l x w x h = 8.24x10^-6 m^3, density = m/V = 8830 kg m^-3. (ii) Calculate density limits (+/-2%) or percentage differences from table values for all three metals; the metal is copper.

items.name: Accurate measurement of position x and resistance R
items.how: Describe how the student could determine accurate values of x and R for a movable copper rod on parallel rails connected to an ohmmeter (Describe, 4 marks).
items.ms: Measure x with a metre rule; keep the movable rod perpendicular (set square), measure on both rods or to the rod centre, view the rule perpendicularly; check ohmmeter zero error, choose a range, or repeat R and average; minimise contact resistance (clean rods).

items.name: Why best-fit line misses the origin
items.how: State why the line of best fit on the R against x graph does not pass through the origin (State, 1 mark).
items.ms: Any one: at x = 0 the ohmmeter measures the resistance of the movable rod, zero error of the ohmmeter, or resistance of the connecting leads.

items.name: Copper resistivity from resistance-position graph
items.how: Determine the resistivity of copper using l = 2x + 0.050 m, rod diameter 3.0 mm and the R against x graph (Determine, 4 marks).
items.ms: A = pi r^2 = 7.1x10^-6 m^2; l = 2x + 0.05 m; R = rho l / A using a pair of values from the best-fit line (or gradient = 2 rho / A); rho = 1.7x10^-8 ohm m.

items.name: Effect of rail wear on train position estimate
items.how: Explain how a decrease in rail cross-sectional area affects a position estimate made from resistance (Explain, 2 marks).
items.ms: Smaller cross-sectional area increases the resistance per unit length of track; the system then estimates the train to be further away than it really is (second mark dependent on first).

items.name: Measuring water depth and wave speed accurately
items.how: Describe how to determine accurate values of the water depth d and wave speed v in a 40.0 cm tray using a metre rule and stopwatch (Describe, 4 marks).
items.ms: Keep the metre rule vertical; measure d at several places and average; time the wave over at least two tray lengths (or repeat and average, or film it); v = distance travelled / mean time (e.g. 0.40 m / t).

items.name: Graph for k, criticise data, compare with g
items.how: For v^2 = kd: (i) describe how a graph gives k (2); (ii) comment on the recorded data (1) and (iii) find mean k and compare it with 9.81 (3); text for (ii) and (iii) is truncated in the extract, content taken from the MS.
items.ms: (i) Plot v^2 against d and compare with y = mx; gradient = k (or d against v^2 with gradient 1/k). (ii) One criticism, e.g. inconsistent d.p. for d or s.f. for k, no repeats, too few depths, k = 9.96 wrongly rounded. (iii) Mean k = 9.71 m s^-2, about 1% from 9.81, so k could be the gravitational field strength.

deps.name: Measuring water depth and wave speed accurately

items.name: Plot Emax against 1/wavelength, find Planck constant
items.how: (i) Calculate 1/lambda and plot Emax against 1/lambda (6); (ii) show h = gradient / c from hc/lambda = phi + Emax (Show that, 2); the MS also shows (iii) determine h from the gradient (4) and (iv) percentage difference from the accepted h (2), text not in the extract.
items.ms: (i) 1/lambda to 3 s.f. (1.61 to 2.29 x10^6 m^-1), axes with quantities and units, sensible scales, plotting (2), best-fit line. (ii) Rearrange to Emax = hc(1/lambda) - phi and compare with y = mx + c, so gradient = hc. (iii) Large-triangle gradient (about 1.24x10^-25 J m) / c gives h of 4.0 to 4.3 x10^-34 J s. (iv) Percentage difference from 6.63x10^-34 J s is about 38% (35 to 40%).

items.name: Random and systematic errors, photoelectric experiment
items.how: Suggest a source of error and a realistic procedural modification for one random and one large systematic error in the photocell investigation (Suggest, 4 marks).
items.ms: Random: hard to judge when the current is zero (use a more sensitive ammeter) or background light alters the colour (block it or put the filter directly above the cell). Systematic: filters not monochromatic (use LEDs or a laser) or zero error of ammeter or voltmeter (check zero before use); 1 mark for source and 1 for modification each.

items.name: Vernier uncertainty, zero error, sphere density
items.how: Viscosity experiment, steel sphere diameter measured with vernier calipers: (i) Determine the percentage uncertainty in d = 12.7 mm (2); (ii) Explain another technique for an accurate d (2); the mark scheme also has a part (iii) (3 marks, density of the sphere) that is not in the extracted question text.
items.ms: (i) half resolution 0.05 mm / 12.7 mm x 100 = 0.4% (accept 0.39%). (ii) Check for and correct zero error, to eliminate systematic error (second mark dependent on first). (iii) From MS: use a balance for mass, r = d/2 and V = 4/3 pi r^3, density = m/V.

items.name: Ensuring terminal velocity between rubber bands
items.how: Describe how the student should ensure the steel sphere is at terminal velocity between the rubber bands on a tube of liquid, including any additional apparatus; a labelled diagram of the tube, bands and stopwatch is given.
items.ms: Four marks: metre rule to measure the distance; record the distance or the time for two regions between the bands; a timing technique (start and stop at the same point of the sphere, lap timer, view in slow motion, repeat from same start); relate to terminal velocity (equal distances in equal times, i.e. same velocity in each region).

items.name: Compare measured viscosity with castor oil
items.how: Deduce whether the liquid could be castor oil, given a measured viscosity of 0.72 Pa s with 6% uncertainty and a quoted castor oil value of 0.65 Pa s.
items.ms: Either lower limit 0.72 - 6% = 0.68 Pa s is greater than 0.65, so not castor oil; or percentage difference about 11% (accept 10%) compared with 6% uncertainty, so not castor oil. One mark for the calculation, one for the comparison and conclusion.

items.name: Sealed box circuit and protective resistor
items.how: Sealed box between terminals X and Y with a 6.0 V supply and fixed resistor R: (i) Complete the circuit diagram (2); (ii) Explain why R is needed when the box contains a diode (3); the mark scheme also has a part (iii) (4 marks, choosing a resistor) not in the extracted question text.
items.ms: (i) supply, variable resistor, ammeter in series, voltmeter across the sealed box. (ii) R limits the current / prevents a short circuit, because with reverse connection the diode has low resistance so current would otherwise be very high. (iii) From MS: R = V/I = (6 - 0.7)/0.200 = 27 ohm, then P = V^2/R about 0.85 W, conclude resistor D (options table not extracted).

items.name: Using a K against L graph for ruler mass

items.name: Plot K against L, find gradient and masses
items.how: Moments data for K and L (six pairs): (i) Plot K on y against L on x (5); (ii) Determine the gradient (3); the mark scheme also has (iii) find MB from the gradient (2) and (iv) find MR from the y-intercept (4), not in the extracted text.
