items.name: Lens refractive index and crown glass test
items.how: Given n = 1 + d^2/(8tf) with d = 5.02 +/- 0.02 cm, t = 4.28 +/- 0.01 mm, f = 11.6 +/- 0.2 cm: (i) determine n (2); per MS also (ii) percentage uncertainty in n (2) and (iii) decide whether the lens could be crown glass, n = 1.52 (2).
items.ms: (i) Substitute with consistent units, n = 1.63 to 3 s.f. (ii) 2 x %U in d plus %U in t and f gives about 1% (1.1%; 0.9% by max/min). (iii) Lower limit 1.61 (or %D 7.2% against %U) is above 1.52, so the lens could not be crown glass (conclusion dependent).

deps.name: Uncertainty in lens focal length

items.name: Period from oscilloscope pulse train
items.how: Describe how to determine the time period of a rotating wheel from a series of pulses shown on an oscilloscope screen.
items.ms: Measure the number of divisions between the same points on the pulses (1); multiply by time per division (1); measure first to last pulse and divide by the number of intervals, or average successive intervals (1).

items.name: Choosing oscilloscope time base for wheel
items.how: Magnet speed 22.2 m s^-1 and wheel diameter 25.4 cm: explain which of the listed ms-per-division settings (table not in the extracted text) would show two complete pulses.
items.ms: Use T = 2 pi/omega with v = omega r (1); T = 35.9 ms (1); time per division from T and screen width, 10 divisions so at least 3.59 ms per division (1); valid choice, 5 ms per division rather than 2 ms per division (1).

items.name: Plan to find latent heat of vaporisation
items.how: Devise a plan, using a graphical method, to determine L for water boiled by a 12 V d.c. heater on a balance, including a circuit diagram and extra apparatus.
items.ms: Circuit with d.c. supply, voltmeter and ammeter (or joulemeter/wattmeter) (1); wait until the water boils (1); record mass m (1) at times t with a stopwatch or at energies E with a joulemeter (1); plot a suitable graph, e.g. m against t (gradient VI/L) or m against VIt (gradient 1/L) (1); use the gradient to obtain L (1).

items.name: Error source affecting latent heat value
items.how: Given mass-reading fluctuation as one significant error, explain how another significant source of error affects the value of L.
items.ms: Identify a significant error, e.g. energy transferred to the surroundings (1); effect, less energy reaches the water per second (1); so L is too large (1, dependent). Any reasonable source of error in the experiment accepted.

items.name: Timing trolley oscillations accurately
items.how: Trolley oscillating between two springs: (i) describe how to modify the equipment so timing is as accurate as possible (2); (ii) describe two techniques to reduce uncertainty in T (2; text partly truncated in the extract).
items.ms: (i) Place a timing marker on the bench directly below a specific point of the trolley at equilibrium (1+1). (ii) Any two of: time multiple oscillations and divide, repeat and calculate a mean, start timing after several oscillations (credit reference to the stationary marker).

items.name: Log graph for trolley period, validity and k
items.how: Six pairs of M and T: (i) plot log T against log M with processed columns (6); (ii) discuss the validity of T = 2 pi sqrt(M/k) (5); per MS also (iii) determine k from the graph (3; not in the extracted text).
items.ms: (i) log values to 2 d.p., axes log(T/s) and log(M/kg), appropriate scales, accurate plots, best-fit line. (ii) log T = log(2 pi/sqrt k) + 0.5 log M so gradient should be 0.5 (2), large-triangle gradient 0.47 to 0.54 (2), conclude the prediction is valid (1). (iii) Read the y-intercept, antilog to get 2 pi/sqrt k, k about 50 to 54 kg s^-2 (= N m^-1) (3).

items.name: Lens diameter instrument choice, precision versus accuracy
items.how: (i) State with a reason whether Vernier calipers or a micrometer should measure a lens diameter of about 5 cm (1); (ii) explain why three precise readings (5.10, 5.11, 5.10 cm) need not be accurate (2).
items.ms: (i) Vernier calipers, as the micrometer range (about 25 mm) is too small (1). (ii) There may be a systematic or zero error (1), so readings may not be close to the true value or have a constant offset (1).

items.name: Mean lens edge thickness and uncertainty
items.how: Calculate the mean and uncertainty of five micrometer readings of the lens edge thickness x (2.11, 2.10, 2.13, 2.14, 2.11 mm).
items.ms: Mean x = 2.12 mm (1); uncertainty 0.02 mm from half range, or furthest from the mean (1).

items.name: Lens refractive index, uncertainty, glass identification
items.how: Given n = 1 + [d^2 + (t-x)^2]/[8f(t-x)] with d = 5.10 +/- 0.01 cm, t = 8.30 +/- 0.01 mm, f = 9.8 +/- 0.3 cm: (i) determine n (2); per MS also (ii) %U in (t-x) (2), (iii) uncertainty in d^2 + (t-x)^2 (4), (iv) %U in n and which glass the lens is (3).
items.ms: (i) Substitute using x from (b), n = 1.54 (2). (ii) Add U in t and x (0.03 mm), %U about 0.49% (2). (iii) Double the %U for d and (t-x), find each absolute uncertainty and add, 0.106 (4); erratum says the printed unit (cm) should have been cm^2 and a square-rooted answer is still credited. (iv) Total %U about 3.95%, limits 1.48 to 1.60, crown glass (n = 1.52) is the only listed value inside (or %D comparison), conclusion dependent (3).

deps.name: Mean lens edge thickness and uncertainty

items.name: Thermometer resolution and fixed temperature intervals
items.how: Kitchen thermometer scale shown: (i) state its resolution in deg C (1); (ii) explain why timing at fixed temperature intervals is better than recording temperature at fixed time intervals (2).
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: (i) resolution is the scale division, not a reading or the range. (ii) The resolution is relatively large, so temperature read at fixed times would carry a large uncertainty; fixed temperature steps avoid this.

items.name: Control variable and sketch for greater specific heat
items.how: Investigation repeated with a different liquid from the same initial temperature: (i) state another control variable (1); (ii) sketch the temperature-time line for a liquid with greater specific heat capacity on the given graph (2).
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: (i) mass of liquid, not volume. (ii) Curve starting at the same point as the original and lying below it, curved rather than straight.

items.name: Data logger benefits for heating liquid
items.how: Give two reasons why a temperature probe connected to a data logger would improve the steam-heating investigation.
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: context-specific reasons, e.g. temperature and time can be recorded simultaneously, and many more readings can be taken in a short time when temperature changes quickly; generic reaction time or automatic graph points are not enough.

items.name: Plan to test coupled pendulum power law
items.how: Devise a plan to test P = a L^b by a graphical method for two coupled pendulums, where P is the time for one pendulum's amplitude to go from zero to maximum and back to zero.
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: first four marks for measurements and analysis (metre rule for L, instruments, number of sets of data, log graph checked for a straight line or constant gradient); last two for any two of three techniques (metre rule vertical, time several cycles of energy transfer, repeat and average at fixed L).

items.name: Video recording to improve measurement of P
items.how: Suggest how recording the pendulums with a video camera may improve the measurement of P.
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: reaction-time remarks accepted only if linked to the experiment, e.g. replaying in slow motion to judge accurately when amplitude is zero or maximum since changes happen quickly.

items.name: Why log Z against log f is straight
items.how: Explain why a graph of log Z against log f would give a straight line, given Z = k f^n for the most intense spectral line.
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: correct log expansion log Z = log k + n log f (1); compare with y = mx + c in the same order and state that the gradient is constant (1), not just that the gradient is n.

items.name: Nut diameter: calipers choice, technique, mean
items.how: Hole diameter d of a hexagonal nut: (i) explain with calculations why digital calipers (mm) are better than Vernier calipers (cm) using the photographed readings (4); per the Examiners' Report also (ii) explain another technique for digital calipers (2) and (iii) mean and uncertainty of repeat readings (3).
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: (i) percentage uncertainty from half the resolution for each instrument, smaller for the digital calipers, then a comparison (4). (ii) Repeat at different orientations and average (random error) or check and correct zero error (systematic error), linked to the error type. (iii) Mean to the same d.p., half range shown, uncertainty to the same d.p.

items.name: Uncertainty in nut area
items.how: Show that the uncertainty in the shaded area A of the nut (formula in s^2 and d^2; s = 16.83 +/- 0.02 mm, d = 8.55 +/- 0.04 mm, A = 1.88 cm^2) is about 0.01 cm^2.
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: three method marks (percentage uncertainties or max/min for s^2 and d^2, convert to absolute uncertainties with the formula's scaling factors, convert mm^2 to cm^2) and a final value given to one more figure than 0.01 cm^2.

items.name: Nut density and steel comparison
items.how: Given m = 10.3 +/- 0.1 g, x = 7.92 +/- 0.03 mm and A = 1.88 +/- 0.01 cm^2: (i) determine the density (2); per the Examiners' Report also (ii) deduce whether the nut could be steel given a density range (3).
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: (i) convert units, rho = m/(A x), answer to 3 s.f. (ii) Combine percentage uncertainties (or max/min, or %D against %U), find the relevant limit and compare it explicitly with the steel range before concluding.

deps.name: Uncertainty in nut area

items.name: Spectral line log graph, n and k + Does graph support Moseley relationship
items.how: Explain whether the graph supports Moseley's suggestion that Z is proportional to f^0.5.
items.ms: No mark scheme in file (Examiners' Report only). Report: use features of the graph, i.e. state that the gradient n should be 0.5, give the measured gradient and compare, then conclude; a bare 'n is close to 0.5' scores nothing.

items.name: Method for volume flow rate of water
items.how: Describe a simple method to determine the volume flow rate of water leaving a tube from a water tank.
items.ms: Either time the flow for a known volume or measure the volume for a known time (2 marks), then use volume flow rate = volume / time (1).

items.name: Pulse frequency from oscilloscope trace
items.how: Oscilloscope trace of pulses from a paddle-wheel magnet and coil, time base 50 ms per division (trace in figure): calculate the frequency f of the pulses.
items.ms: Number of divisions x 50 ms per division (1); use f = 1/T (1); f = 6.3 Hz (6.25 Hz accepted) (1). Example: 6.4 divisions for 2T, T = 0.16 s.

items.name: Plan: pulse frequency against flow rate
items.how: Describe how the student could investigate how the pulse frequency f varies with the volume flow rate of the water.
items.ms: Measure flow rate and frequency at the same height h (1); repeat for different values of h (1); plot a graph of flow rate against f (1).

deps.name: Method for volume flow rate of water
Pulse frequency from oscilloscope trace

items.name: Data logger for overnight river monitoring
items.how: Give two reasons why a data logger is appropriate for monitoring river flow overnight via the pulse frequency.
items.ms: Can be used remotely without monitoring (1); can record over a long period or store a large amount of data (1).

items.name: Safety precautions for beta source
items.how: State two safety precautions for a beta absorption experiment using a source, aluminium sheets and a G-M tube.
items.ms: Any two of: do not point the source at the body, keep a safe distance, use the source for as short a time as possible, handle with tongs. PPE, shielding and storage answers are ignored.

items.name: Beta absorption: ln graph and test plan
items.how: Test C = C0 e^(-mu x) for beta absorption: (i) explain why a graph of ln C against x tests the relationship (2); per MS also (ii) describe the method (6; not in the extracted text).
items.ms: (i) ln C = ln C0 - mu x (1); compare with y = c + mx, gradient -mu constant (1, dependent). (ii) Micrometer for thickness x; record count rate over a long time; at least 5 thicknesses; constant source-detector distance; plus any two of: thickness at several places and mean, correct zero error, subtract background count rate.

items.name: Measuring beam displacement with 15 cm ruler
items.how: Describe an accurate method to determine a single value of the beam centre displacement d using a 15 cm ruler, including any additional apparatus.
items.ms: Record the initial and final positions of the beam centre and subtract (1); plus any two of: set square to keep the ruler vertical, clamp the ruler, read perpendicular to the scale or keep the ruler close to the beam.

items.name: Log graph of beam displacement against length
items.how: Six pairs of support separation L and displacement d: (i) plot log d against log L with processed columns (6); (ii) determine the gradient (3); per MS also (iii) find r and k in d = k L^r (3; not in the extracted text).
items.ms: (i) log values to 3 d.p. (2 d.p. accepted), axes log(d/m) and log(L/m), sensible scales, accurate plots, best-fit line. (ii) Large triangle, gradient 2.75 to 2.95 (about 2.9), positive, 2 or 3 s.f., no unit. (iii) log k from the y-intercept or from gradient plus a point (ecf), convert to k (about 0.0186), state the relationship with r and k.

items.name: Floating test tube timing and mean period
items.how: Floating test tube oscillating vertically: (i) describe two techniques, other than repeating and averaging, to determine T with a stopwatch (2); per MS also (ii) mean T and its uncertainty from repeated timings (3; not in the extracted text).
items.ms: (i) Any two of: time multiple oscillations and divide, use a fiducial marker, let oscillations settle before timing. (ii) Mean T = 0.68 s (1), half range or furthest from mean shown (1), uncertainty 0.02 s with d.p. consistent with the mean (1).

items.name: Vernier calipers suitability for tube diameter
items.how: Explain, with a calculation, why vernier calipers are suitable for measuring a test-tube diameter of about 2 cm.
items.ms: Resolution 0.1 mm or uncertainty 0.05 mm (1); percentage uncertainty 0.05/20 = 0.25%, which is small (1). Precision or accuracy are not accepted in place of resolution.

items.name: Liquid density, uncertainty and glycerol test
items.how: Given T = sqrt(16 pi m/(D^2 rho g)), D = 2.38 +/- 0.01 cm, T = 0.61 +/- 0.01 s, m = 48.95 g: (i) show rho is about 1200 kg m^-3 (2); per MS also (ii) percentage uncertainty in rho (3) and (iii) whether the liquid could be glycerol, 1260 kg m^-3 (2).
items.ms: (i) Rearrange to rho = 16 pi m/(D^2 T^2 g) (1), substitute in SI units to get 1190 kg m^-3 (1). (ii) 2 x %U in D plus 2 x %U in T, about 4.1% (or max/min with half range). (iii) Upper limit 1239 kg m^-3 (or %D 5.6% against %U) is below 1260, so the liquid may not be glycerol (conclusion dependent).

items.name: Safety precautions for capacitor circuit
items.how: State two safety precautions when connecting and using a circuit with an electrolytic capacitor discharging through a motor.
items.ms: Any two of: connect the capacitor with the correct polarity, do not exceed its working p.d., ensure it is fully discharged when handling.

items.name: Measuring lifted height with metre rule
items.how: Describe an accurate method to determine a single value of the height h through which the motor lifts a mass, using a metre rule and any extra apparatus.
items.ms: Clamp the rule and use a set square or spirit level to make it vertical (1); rule close to the mass (1); view perpendicular to the scale or use a set square to read it (1).

items.name: Mean lift height, uncertainty and efficiency
items.how: Four repeat readings of h: (i) calculate the mean (1); (ii) determine the percentage uncertainty in the mean (2); per MS also (iii) efficiency of the energy transfer, comparing E = 1/2 C V^2 with mgh (3; not in the extracted text).
items.ms: (i) 0.242 m to 3 d.p. (1). (ii) Half range 3.5 mm shown (1), %U = 1.4% to 1 or 2 s.f. (1.7% if furthest from mean used). (iii) Use E = 1/2 C V^2 and E = mgh (1), efficiency = useful output / total input (1), efficiency 0.56 or 56% (1).

items.name: Show viscosity unit from flow formula
items.how: Show that the formula M = pi rho P r^4 t/(8 eta L) gives the unit of viscosity eta as N s m^-2.
items.ms: Substitute units for all variables (1); clear working leading to N s m^-2 (1), e.g. (kg m^-3)(N m^-2)(m^4)(s) over (m)(kg).

items.name: Plan to find viscosity using graph
items.how: Describe a method, using a suitable graph, to determine an accurate value of viscosity eta from water flowing through a horizontal pipe, with a metre rule for L and a stopwatch for t.
items.ms: Six points: internal diameter with vernier calipers; repeat at different orientations and average; one of pipe horizontal (spirit level), constant pressure difference, or stopwatch near the balance; measure M and corresponding t; at least 5 sets; plot M against t and use the gradient to find eta (valid alternative graphs accepted).

items.name: Data logger benefits for mass balance
items.how: Give two reasons why connecting the mass balance to a data logger would improve the flow investigation.
items.ms: Mass and time are recorded simultaneously (1); the data logger has a high sampling rate (1).

items.name: Accurate period of rotational oscillation
items.how: Describe how to determine an accurate value of T for rotational oscillations of a mass on a spring, using a stopwatch.
items.ms: Time multiple oscillations and divide (1); marker at the centre of the oscillation or on the mass (1); repeat T and calculate a mean, or allow oscillations to settle before timing (1).

items.name: Log graph of T against M, b and a
items.how: Given T = a M^b: (i) explain how a graph of log T against log M gives b (2); per MS also (ii) plot the graph from a table of M and T (6), (iii) determine the gradient (3) and (iv) determine a (3); only (i) is in the extracted question text.
items.ms: (i) log T = log a + b log M (1); compare with y = c + mx, b is the constant gradient (1, dependent). (ii) log values to 3 d.p. (2 d.p. allowed), axes log(T/s) and log(M/kg), sensible scales, accurate plots, best-fit line. (iii) Large triangle, gradient 0.51 to 0.55, positive, 2 or 3 s.f., no unit. (iv) y-intercept read or calculated (1), antilog (1), a about 3.43 to 2 or 3 s.f., unit s allowed (1).

items.name: Micrometer technique and suitability for thickness
items.how: (i) Explain one technique for measuring protractor thickness t with a micrometer screw gauge (2); per MS also (ii) explain with a percentage-uncertainty calculation why the micrometer suits t = 1.41 mm (2; question text truncated in the extract).
items.ms: (i) Repeat at different places and average (reduces random error) or check and correct zero error (eliminates systematic error), technique then dependent reason. (ii) Resolution 0.01 mm or uncertainty 0.005 mm (1); %U = 0.005/1.41 = 0.35%, which is small (1).

items.name: Protractor volume and its uncertainty
items.how: Semicircle-plus-rectangle protractor with D = 10.10 +/- 0.05 cm, x = 4.5 +/- 0.1 mm, t = 1.40 +/- 0.02 mm: (i) show that V is about 6.2 cm^3 (2); (ii) show that the uncertainty in V is about 0.2 cm^3 (4).
items.ms: (i) V = (semicircle area + rectangle area) x thickness (1), V = 6.24 cm^3 (1). (ii) Percentage uncertainties (2 x %U in D plus %U in t for the semicircle term; %U in D, x, t for the rectangle term), convert to absolute and add, U = 0.16 cm^3; or max and min V (6.40 and 6.08) with half range.

items.name: Density compared with accepted Perspex value
items.how: Density found as 1.04 g cm^-3 with 3% uncertainty against an accepted Perspex value of 1.18 g cm^-3: explain, with a calculation, whether the protractor could be Perspex.
items.ms: Upper limit of density 1.04 x 1.03 = 1.07 g cm^-3 (1); accepted value is larger so it may not be Perspex (1, dependent). Alternative: %D = 12%, greater than the 3% uncertainty.

items.name: Check air track is horizontal
items.how: Describe question: how to show an air track is level before a two-glider, two-light-gate momentum investigation.
items.ms: One mark for any valid safe practical check: glider pushed gently passes both light gates in similar times, or a glider placed on the track stays stationary, or rule/set square shows track height equal in two places, or spirit level bubble central.

items.name: Show momentum conserved from timings
items.how: Show that: given card times t1 and t2 for three collisions of identical gliders that stick together, and that momentum conservation requires t2 = 2 t1.
items.ms: Use t2 = 2 t1 (1); three correct calculations such as t2/t1 = 2.06, 1.86, 1.96 (1); conclusion that ratios are approximately 2 so momentum was conserved (1).

items.name: Assess longer card suggestion
items.how: Assess: whether using a piece of card twice as long would improve the light-gate momentum investigation.
items.ms: Time through the gate should double (1); timer resolution/uncertainty is constant (1); so the percentage uncertainty in the time halves, improving the investigation (1).

items.name: Plan alpha particle range in air
items.how: Devise a more detailed plan (6 marks) improving a four-line outline for finding how far alpha particles travel in air using a source and Geiger-Muller tube.
items.ms: Any six from: measure and subtract background count (rate); source and detector in line; metre rule for d; repeat counts and take a mean or count for a long time; vary d up to about 50 mm or until count reaches background; plot corrected count (rate) against d; sensible safety comment (distance, shielding or time).

items.name: Accurate timing of magnet oscillations
items.how: Describe how to measure the time period of an oscillating suspended bar magnet as accurately as possible.
items.ms: Any three: time multiple oscillations and divide by the number; repeat and calculate a mean; use a timing marker at the centre of the oscillation; start timing after several oscillations have completed.

items.name: Testing predicted T against I relationship
items.how: Two short parts: (i) State the extra circuit component needed to vary the current I (1); (ii) Explain why a graph of log T against log I tests the predicted power relationship (2).
items.ms: (i) Variable resistor (1). (ii) log T = n log I is of the form y = mx (+ c) (1), so if the relationship is valid the graph is a straight line (through the origin) with gradient n (1).

items.name: Log-log graph and exponent n
items.how: Process six T and I readings into log T and log I, plot the graph (6) and use it to determine n (3); the mark scheme also has a 4-mark part (iii) that is not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Log values to at least 2 d.p. (2), axes log(T/s) and log(I/A) (1), appropriate scales (1), plots within 1 mm (1), best-fit line (1). (ii) Gradient from a large triangle, n of magnitude 0.49 to 0.53 (example -0.498), negative, 2 or 3 s.f., no unit (3). (iii) log T = n log I + log k is y = mx + c; a non-zero intercept means k is not 1 (4).

deps.name: Testing predicted T against I relationship

items.name: Slot dimensions and area uncertainty
items.how: (i) Name the most appropriate instrument for the slot width and length (1); (ii) explain one measuring technique (2); the mark scheme also has a 3-mark part (iii) for the slot area and its uncertainty that is not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Digital or vernier calipers. (ii) A pair: check for zero error to eliminate systematic error, or repeat at different places and average to reduce random error. (iii) Area a x b = 1.03 cm^2, %U = 0.01/0.47 + 0.005/2.19 = 2.4%, U = 0.02 cm^2 (3).

items.name: Shaded area of slotted mass
items.how: Calculate the shaded area (whole disc of diameter 3.81 cm minus the slot) (2), then calculate the uncertainty in that area (3).
items.ms: (i) Use area = pi d^2/4 = 11.4 cm^2 and subtract slot area 1.03 cm^2 to get 10.4 cm^2 (2). (ii) %U in d from 0.005/3.81, doubled for d^2 (0.26%), giving 0.03 cm^2; add the slot uncertainty 0.02 cm^2 to get 0.05 cm^2 (3).

deps.name: Slot dimensions and area uncertainty

items.name: Density of metal and uncertainty
items.how: (i) Calculate the density in g cm^-3 from 100 g and the volume (shaded area x mean thickness from micrometer readings) (2); the mark scheme also has a 3-mark part (ii) on the percentage uncertainty in density.
items.ms: (i) Use density = m/V with V = 10.4 cm^2 x 1.137 cm, giving 8.47 g cm^-3 (2, ecf). (ii) Half-range in t 0.02 mm gives 0.18%, shaded area 0.48%, added to give 0.66% (3).

deps.name: Shaded area of slotted mass

items.name: Could the mass be brass
items.how: Determine whether the measured density (with its uncertainty) allows the slotted mass to be brass of density 8.5 g cm^-3.
items.ms: Either calculate the density range (8.47 +/- 0.06, i.e. 8.41 to 8.53 g cm^-3) and note brass lies inside it, or calculate %D = 0.35% and compare with %U = 0.66%; conclude it could be brass (1 + 1, ecf).

deps.name: Density of metal and uncertainty

items.name: Control variables and criticising heating data
items.how: (i) Identify two other control variables for the resistor-heating-water investigation (2); (ii) criticise the recording of a table of current I and temperature rise (3).
items.ms: (i) Two of: mass or volume of water; time (or distance between resistor and thermometer). (ii) Inconsistent significant figures; not enough sets of readings or no repeats; no unit for the temperature rise or initial and final temperatures not recorded (1 each).

items.name: Reducing uncertainty in temperature rise
items.how: Explain one improvement the student could make to reduce the uncertainty in the temperature rise for each current.
items.ms: A pair: insulate or cover the beaker (1) to reduce energy transfer to surroundings (1); or stir the water or place the thermometer close to the resistor (1) so the water is at the same temperature as the resistor (1). Second mark depends on the first.

items.name: Period of pendulum with peg
items.how: Determine the time period of the whole oscillation of a pendulum (l = 1.00 m) whose string hits a peg 0.25 m below the pivot.
items.ms: Use T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g) (1); add half the period of the long pendulum (2.01 s) and half the period of the short 0.75 m pendulum (1.74 s) (1); T = 1.9 s, 2 or 3 s.f. (1). Bald answer scores only the last mark.

items.name: Plan graph test of peg pendulum
items.how: Devise a plan (6 marks) using a stopwatch and any extra apparatus to test a suggested approximate relationship between T and peg depth h with a graphical method.
items.ms: Metre rule to measure h (1); any three of: timing marker at centre of oscillation, small initial angle, time several oscillations and divide, repeat and mean, start timing after several oscillations (3); at least five values of h (1); plot T^2 against h (or valid alternative) and check for a straight line (1).

items.name: Light gate versus stopwatch timing
items.how: Discuss whether timing the pendulum with a light gate and data logger would improve the investigation planned in (b).
items.ms: Light gate eliminates reaction time (1); plus either fixed position removes parallax (1, 1), or the gate times from the edge of the bob rather than its centre of mass, adding uncertainty in the period (1, 1).

deps.name: Plan graph test of peg pendulum

items.name: Finding resonant frequency with oscilloscope
items.how: Describe how the student should use the oscilloscope trace (microphone signal near a bottle and loudspeaker) to identify the resonant frequency and determine its value.
items.ms: Adjust the signal generator to get the trace of maximum amplitude (1); count divisions between two adjacent peaks (1); multiply by the time per division to get the period (1); calculate frequency as 1/T (1).

items.name: Log-log graph of frequency against volume
items.how: (i) Plot log f against log V from six pairs of air volume and resonant frequency, recording processed data (6); (ii) discuss whether the graph supports f = kV^(-1/2) (5).
items.ms: (i) Log values to 2 d.p. for both V and f (2), axes log(f/Hz) and log(V/cm^3) (1), correct scales (1), plots within 1 mm (1), best-fit line (1); ln-ln accepted. (ii) log f = log k - 1/2 log V so gradient -1/2 (2); gradient from large triangle (1); value -0.51 to -0.54 (1); valid conclusion comparing with -1/2 (1).

items.name: Measuring rod end heights p and q
items.how: (i) Describe two techniques for measuring heights p and q with a metre rule (2); the mark scheme also has a 2-mark part (ii) on the uncertainty in the difference of p and q that is not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Two of: keep metre rule vertical using a set square; rod end close to the rule or use a set square to read off; read perpendicular to the scale to avoid parallax. (ii) Single-reading uncertainty is half the resolution (0.5 mm), and the uncertainties add when the two readings are subtracted.

items.name: Measuring rod diameter instrument and technique + Calculating shear modulus of steel + Identifying steel type from G
items.how: Deduce whether the data and G value from part (c) allow the student to tell structural steel (79.3 x 10^9) from carbon steel (77.0 x 10^9 N m^-2).
items.ms: Combine percentage uncertainties using 2 x %U in x and 4 x %U in d (total about 9.4%) (2); find limits 71.3 to 86.1 x 10^9 N m^-2 (or %D of 0.76% and 2.3% against %U) (1); both steels lie within range so the type cannot be determined (1).

items.name: Safety issue with a.c. coil circuit
items.how: Describe one safety issue and how it should be dealt with for a coil connected to an a.c. power supply.
items.ms: A pair (1 + 1): short circuit across supply - use insulated wire; risk of electrocution - use a low p.d.; wire overheating if current too high - use a low p.d. or a limiting resistor.

items.name: Vernier calipers versus metre rule for r
items.how: Explain, including calculations, why vernier calipers are better than a metre rule for measuring a coil separation r between 2 cm and 10 cm.
items.ms: Calipers have higher resolution (0.1 mm against 1 mm for the rule) (1); use half the resolution to find uncertainty or %U (1); valid comparison of %U, e.g. 0.25% against 2.5% at r = 2 cm (1, dependent on an earlier mark).

items.name: Reading maximum emf from oscilloscope
items.how: Describe how to determine an accurate maximum e.m.f. from an a.c. trace on an oscilloscope with y-scale 100 mV per division.
items.ms: Measure the amplitude in divisions (or divisions from maximum to minimum, halved) (1); multiply by 100 mV per division (1); repeat the amplitude measurement and calculate a mean (1).

items.name: Criticising recorded separation and emf data
items.how: Criticise the recording of a table giving r in cm (vernier calipers) and maximum E in V.
items.ms: Any two: inconsistent significant figures or decimal places for E; r not to the correct number of decimal places for the calipers; incorrect units for E; no repeats or not enough readings.

items.name: Why plot ln V against t
items.how: Explain why a graph of ln V against t should be used to test V = V0 e^(-bt) for liquid draining from a tube.
items.ms: ln V = ln V0 - bt is in the form y = c + mx (1), with constant gradient -b, so a valid relationship gives a straight line (1, dependent on the first).

items.name: Obtaining accurate volume and time data
items.how: Describe how to obtain an accurate set of values for V and t to test the exponential relationship for liquid draining through a tap.
items.ms: Open tap and start timing together (1); record volumes at successive time intervals or times to fall to set volumes (1); read to the bottom of the meniscus (1); any one of: tube vertical, stopwatch or lap timer, stopwatch close to tube, refill to same volume and repeat for mean, many readings, tap opened to same position (1).

items.name: Source of uncertainty in draining experiment
items.how: Explain a source of uncertainty in the draining-tube investigation.
items.ms: A pair (1 + 1): hard to read V and t simultaneously, affecting random error; or liquid below the scale, introducing systematic error; or air trapped in the tap, affecting random error.

items.name: Log P against 1/T graph and gradient
items.how: From six saturated vapour pressure and temperature pairs: (i) plot log P against 1/T, recording processed data (6); (ii) determine the gradient (3); the mark scheme also has a 3-mark part (iii) not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) log P to 2 d.p., 1/T to 5 d.p. (or 2 d.p. in standard form), axes log(P/kPa) and 1/T in K^-1, appropriate scales, accurate plots, best-fit line (1 each). (ii) Large-triangle gradient of about -2.2 x 10^3, negative, 2 or 3 s.f. (3). (iii) Gradient used with 2.30k to find X = 7.08 x 10^-20 J (3).

items.name: Boiling point at 100 kPa from graph
items.how: Determine the boiling point in degrees Celsius when atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa, using the saturated vapour pressure data.
items.ms: Interpolate 1/T from the graph at log P = log 100 = 2 (1); invert to find T (about 364 K) (1); convert to Celsius, about 91 C, to 2 or 3 s.f. (1).

deps.name: Log P against 1/T graph and gradient

items.name: Wire diameter micrometer technique and mean
items.how: (i) Explain one technique for measuring the diameter of wire X with a micrometer (2); the mark scheme also has a 3-mark part (ii) for the mean diameter and its uncertainty from five readings (not in extracted text).
items.ms: (i) Repeat at different orientations along the wire and average (reduces random error), or check and correct zero error (eliminates systematic error). (ii) Mean d = 0.31 mm; half-range uncertainty 0.02 mm with decimal places consistent with the mean (3).

items.name: Resistivity of wire Y and uncertainty
items.how: (i) Show that resistivity is about 5 x 10^-7 ohm m from V, I, length and diameter with their uncertainties (3); the mark scheme also has a 3-mark part (ii) on the percentage uncertainty in resistivity.
items.ms: (i) A = pi d^2/4 and R = V/I (1); R = rho L/A rearranged (1); rho = 4.6 x 10^-7 ohm m (1). (ii) 2 x %U in d plus %U in V, I and L, about 9.4% (or max/min method, about 9.3%) (3).

items.name: Uncertainty in resistance per metre
items.how: Show that the percentage uncertainty in R_L = 2(R2 - R1) is about 2%, given single ohmmeter readings for two lengths of wire Y.
items.ms: Use an uncertainty of 0.05 ohm in each of R1 and R2 (1); U = 2 x (U in R2 + U in R1) = 0.2 ohm, or max/min values (1); %U = 0.2/11.4 = 1.8% (1).

items.name: Does data confirm constantan wire
items.how: Comment, with calculations, on how well calculated rho (4.6 x 10^-7 ohm m, 9%) and R_L (11.4 ohm, 2%) confirm the wire is constantan, given published values.
items.ms: Calculate the upper limit of rho (5.0 x 10^-7) and lower limit of R_L (11.2 ohm) (1 + 1), or %D of 6.1% and 1.8%; conclude by comparing limits with published values (or %D with %U) that both agree, so consistent with constantan (1).

deps.name: Resistivity of wire Y and uncertainty
Uncertainty in resistance per metre

items.name: Safety issue with current-carrying wire
items.how: Describe one safety issue and how it should be dealt with when a current of up to 5 A flows in a copper wire between magnets.
items.ms: A pair (1 + 1): wire gets hot - switch off between readings or add a resistor; short circuit - add a resistor; risk of electric shock - use insulated wire.

items.name: Complete circuit diagram for force investigation
items.how: Complete a given circuit diagram so the current in the copper wire can be varied and measured for the top-pan-balance investigation.
items.ms: d.c. power supply and ammeter in series with the copper wire (1); a means of varying the current, e.g. a variable resistor (1). Additional components that do not stop the circuit working are ignored.

items.name: Critique mass against current conclusion
items.how: Explain why the student's conclusion that his m against I graph supports m = BLI/g may not be correct, referring to his readings.
items.ms: Not enough readings (1); range of current too small (1); relationship predicts a straight line through the origin, y = mx (1); so an accurate best-fit line, straight line, zero intercept or direct proportionality cannot be confirmed (1).

items.name: Derive T squared against h relationship
items.how: Show that for a pendulum hanging from a ceiling of height H, T^2 = 4 pi^2 H/g - 4 pi^2 h/g, where h is the height of the sphere centre above the floor.
items.ms: Use T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g) with l = H - h (1); clear algebra leading to the given formula (1).

items.name: Plan to find ceiling height with pendulum
items.how: Describe a method using a stopwatch and the pendulum, based on a suitable graph, to obtain a value for the ceiling height H.
items.ms: Metre rule to measure h (1); keep rule vertical with a set square or measure to bottom of bob and add radius (1); timing marker at centre (1); time multiple oscillations or repeat for a mean or start timing once settled (1); at least five values of h (1); plot T^2 against h and use the intercept to calculate H (1).

deps.name: Derive T squared against h relationship

items.name: Video recording improves pendulum timing
items.how: Explain how a video recording may improve the stopwatch method for finding the pendulum period.
items.ms: The recording can be viewed in slow motion (1), so judging when an oscillation is complete is more accurate (1).

deps.name: Plan to find ceiling height with pendulum

items.name: Why ln P against h gives b
items.how: Explain why a graph of ln P against h can be used to find b in P = P0 e^(-bh).
items.ms: ln P = ln P0 - bh compared with y = c + mx (1); gradient is -b, which is constant (1, dependent on the first).

items.name: ln P against height graph and applications
items.how: (i) Plot ln P against h from six pressure and height readings, recording processed data (5); (ii) determine the gradient (3); the mark scheme also has (iii) a 3-mark part using the gradient to find M and (iv) a 3-mark extrapolation to a negative height, neither in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) ln P consistent to 3 d.p., axes ln(P/kPa) and h/m, appropriate scales, accurate plots, best-fit line. (ii) Large triangle, gradient -1.20 to -1.30 x 10^-4, negative, 2 or 3 s.f. (3). (iii) Gradient used to give M = 5.02 x 10^-26 kg (3). (iv) y-intercept ln P0 about 4.62, extrapolate to h = -414 m to get P of 105 to 108 kPa (3).

items.name: Rubber band thickness with micrometer
items.how: (i) Explain one technique for measuring thickness t with a micrometer (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) mean t (1), (iii) percentage uncertainty in t (2), (iv) why a larger measurement reduces %U (2) and (v) a reason the band's length or width may be measured inaccurately (2), not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Repeat at different places and average, or use the ratchet to avoid squashing rubber, or check and correct zero error, each with the matching error type. (ii) Mean t = 1.04 mm. (iii) Half-range 0.03 mm gives about 3%. (iv) Same uncertainty on a larger measurement so %U falls. (v) Fold at the ends ignored, or band not taut or compressed.

items.name: Uncertainty in D squared and bung area
items.how: (i) Show that the uncertainty in D^2 is about 0.07 cm^2 given D = 3.45 +/- 0.01 cm (2); the mark scheme also has a 2-mark part (ii) for the uncertainty in the bung's cross-sectional area A.
items.ms: (i) Use 2 x %U in D (0.58%) times D^2 to get 0.069 cm^2, or take the half-range of D^2 (2). (ii) Add the uncertainties of the terms in A and apply the formula's constant factor to get 0.052 cm^2 (2 s.f.), or use maximum and minimum A (0.053 cm^2) (2).

items.name: Same rubber for band and bung
items.how: Deduce whether a rubber band (1.15 g cm^-3, 4.3%) and a rubber bung (1.52 g cm^-3, 1.2%) could be the same type of rubber.
items.ms: Calculate a relevant limit or uncertainty from the percentage uncertainty (1); upper limit for band 1.20 and lower limit for bung 1.50 g cm^-3 (1); ranges do not overlap so not the same rubber (1).

items.name: Safety issue heating diode in water
items.how: Identify one health and safety issue and how it should be dealt with when heating a diode in a beaker of water on a hotplate.
items.ms: A pair (1 + 1): hot beaker or water causes burns or spills - use tongs or insulated gloves; hot plate causes burns - turn it off or use gloves; short circuit - insulate leads (not low p.d.); leads pull beaker over - clamp the leads.

items.name: Why include variable resistor with diode
items.how: Explain why the student was correct to include a variable resistor in a circuit used to measure diode current as temperature changes.
items.ms: To keep the potential difference across the diode constant (1), because the resistance of the diode or circuit may change with temperature (1).

items.name: Current unit check and data range
items.how: (i) Explain, with a suitable calculation, whether the unit for current in the table is correct (3); the mark scheme also has a 2-mark part (ii) on why the data cannot test the predicted linear variation.
items.ms: (i) Use R = V/I with the 6 V supply and circuit resistance (1); find I in the range 5.5 x 10^-3 A to 0.060 A (or V 430 to 900 V, or R 0.67 to 1.4 ohm) (1); conclusion comparing calculated value with the table values or 6 V (1). (ii) Not enough sets of data; temperature range too small (data needed below 29.5 C or above 50 C).

deps.name: Why include variable resistor with diode

items.name: Mean period, uncertainty and timing technique
items.how: (i) Determine the mean period T from four readings of 5T (2); (ii) determine the percentage uncertainty in mean T (2); the mark scheme also has a 3-mark part (iii) on timing technique, not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Mean 5T = 7.55 s, so T = 1.51 s (2). (ii) Half-range 0.13 s over 7.55 s gives 1.7% (2). (iii) Three of: timing marker at centre of oscillation, allow oscillations to settle before timing, small or vertical displacement.

items.name: Plan to find half-amplitude time
items.how: Devise a method, including a suitable graph, to find the time for a damped mass-spring oscillation amplitude to fall to half its initial value, given A = A0 e^(-lambda n).
items.ms: Metre rule to measure amplitude (1); rule clamped close to card, vertical via set square, or viewed perpendicularly (1); record A at known n (1); at least five sets of data (1); plot ln A against n (1); read n at which A halves from the graph (or use gradient with n = ln 2/lambda) and multiply by the period T (1).

deps.name: Mean period, uncertainty and timing technique

items.name: Why log L against log M gives r
items.how: Explain how a graph of log L against log(M/M_sun) can be used to find r in L = L_sun (M/M_sun)^r for main sequence stars.
items.ms: log L = log L_sun + r log(M/M_sun) compared with y = c + mx (1); r is the gradient, which is constant (1, dependent on the first).

items.name: Log-log graph of stellar luminosity against mass
items.how: From six stars' L (in 10^35 W) and M/M_sun: (i) plot log L against log(M/M_sun) without converting L to W (6); (ii) determine r from the graph (3); the mark scheme also has (iii) L_sun (3) and (iv) L for M = 33 M_sun (2), not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Both sets of logs consistent to 3 d.p. (2), axes log(L/10^35 W) and log(M/M_sun) (1), scales (1), plots (1), best-fit line (1). (ii) Large triangle, r of 3.50 to 3.70 (example 3.65), no unit (3). (iii) y-intercept 1.57 gives L_sun about 3.7 x 10^36 W (3). (iv) L = L_sun x 33^r about 1.3 x 10^42 W (2).

items.name: Digital calipers technique for width
items.how: Explain one technique to use when measuring the width a of a wooden metre rule with digital calipers.
items.ms: Either repeat at different places and calculate a mean (orientation not accepted) to reduce random error, or check and correct for zero error to eliminate systematic error (1 + 1; one mark available for the technique alone).

items.name: Young modulus of wooden rule by oscillation
items.how: (i) Explain how increasing the clamp distance D affects the percentage uncertainty in 20T (3); the mark scheme also has (ii) calculate E from given M, D, a, b, T (2), (iii) %U in E (3) and (iv) comparing with the accepted value for beech wood (2), not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) 20T increases (1), its uncertainty stays constant (1), so the percentage uncertainty falls (1). (ii) Substitute into E = 16 pi^2 M D^3/(a b^3 T^2) to get 1.43 x 10^10 Pa (2). (iii) Combine 3 x %U in D, %U in a, 3 x %U in b, 2 x %U in T, about 4.8% (3). (iv) Lower limit about 13.6 GPa lies above beech's value, so not beech (2).
